security_spec.violation_condition: Kernel S-mode code executes CBO management instructions (cbo.clean, cbo.flush, cbo.inval) on a user virtual address without first verifying that the owning user task holds read permission for that page, or executes cbo.zero on a user virtual address without verifying the user holds write permission — relying on the implicit assumption that CBO permission semantics mirror explicit load/store rather than on explicit page-table / PMP checks performed by hardware at the privilege level of execution.
security_spec.summary: CBO management instructions (clean/flush/inval) now explicitly require read permission and cbo.zero requires write permission on the accessed page; kernel S-mode use of these instructions on untrusted user addresses without prior access_ok() or equivalent permission validation can bypass the page-table-enforced security boundary, enabling cache-based side-channel probing via cbo.inval or unauthorized memory zeroing via cbo.zero.

findings.finding: CBO clean operates on kernel virtual address via phys_to_virt(paddr). The paddr comes from DMA mapping infrastructure, not from user virtual addresses. These are kernel-owned DMA buffers with proper page table mappings maintained by the DMA API. No violation of user-page permission semantics.
findings.snippet:
void *vaddr = phys_to_virt(paddr);
ALT_CMO_OP(CLEAN, vaddr, size, riscv_cbom_block_size);

findings.finding: CBO inval operates on kernel virtual address from phys_to_virt(paddr). Same as arch_dma_cache_wback: the physical address originates from DMA-mapped kernel buffers, not userspace.
findings.snippet:
void *vaddr = phys_to_virt(paddr);
ALT_CMO_OP(INVAL, vaddr, size, riscv_cbom_block_size);

findings.finding: CBO flush on kernel virtual address from phys_to_virt. DMA coherent-prep path (arch_dma_prep_coherent, line 117-129) also uses page_address(page) which returns kernel linear-map VA. All are kernel-owned memory.
CBO clean on persistent memory addresses. addr comes from the kernel's direct map (struct page-based PMEM). These are kernel-owned persistent memory regions, not user virtual addresses.
CBO inval on persistent memory - same analysis as arch_wb_cache_pmem. Kernel-owned PMEM addresses only.

CBO zero operates on the kernel linear-map virtual address of page being cleared. The address in a0 is a kernel virtual address, not a user virtual address. On page fault paths, the kernel writes to the page through the linear map where it holds full write permission. The ALTERNATIVE framework correctly: (a) falls back to memset when Zicboz is absent (order=12), (b) selects the proper unrolled loop variant based on riscv_cboz_block_size (orders 6-11=log2(block_size)).
findings.snippet:
CBO_ZERO(a0)
add  a0, a0, a1
CBOZ_ALT(11, "bltu a0, a2, .Lzero_loop; ret", "nop; nop")
// fallback: .Lno_zicboz: li a1, 0; tail __memset

findings.finding: Zicbop prefetch instructions (prefetch.r, prefetch.w) are architecturally defined as HINTs by the RISC-V spec. They are always legal, never raise exceptions, and are semantically NOPs when the address is invalid or the hint is unrecognized. They are categorically distinct from CBO management instructions (cbo.clean/flush/inval/zero) and fall outside the scope of the security spec's vulnerability pattern.
findings.snippet:
ALTERNATIVE(__nops(1), PREFETCH_R(x, 0), 0, RISCV_ISA_EXT_ZICBOP, CONFIG_RISCV_ISA_ZICBOP)
ALTERNATIVE(__nops(1), PREFETCH_W(x, 0), 0, RISCV_ISA_EXT_ZICBOP, CONFIG_RISCV_ISA_ZICBOP)

findings.finding: envcfg CSR is properly switched on context switch. switch_to() macro calls __switch_to_envcfg(next) at line 124, which writes next->thread.envcfg to CSR_ENVCFG. The CBZE and CBCFE bits set during riscv_user_isa_enable() (cpufeature.c:1173-1179) in current->thread.envcfg are thus propagated when that task runs again. No CSR leakage across task boundaries.
envcfg CSR is saved on suspend (line 18) and restored on resume (line 48). This ensures CBO-related envcfg bits (CBZE, CBCFE, CBIE) are preserved across suspend/resume cycles and CPU hotplug.
findings.snippet:
context->envcfg = csr_read(CSR_ENVCFG);  // save
csr_write(CSR_ENVCFG, context->envcfg);   // restore

findings.finding: KVM correctly configures henvcfg for guest CBO delegation. When guest has Zicbom: sets CBIE (cache block invalidate enable) and CBCFE (cache block clean/flush enable) bits. When guest has Zicboz: sets CBZE (cache block zero enable) bit. These are written to the hardware CSR in kvm_arch_vcpu_load (line 596/615). Guest CBO instructions are either allowed by hardware or trap as illegal instructions redirected back to the guest (truly_illegal_insn in vcpu_insn.c:30-44).

On VCPU enter, host senvcfg is swapped out (saved to vcpu->arch.host_senvcfg) and guest senvcfg is swapped in (csr->senvcfg written to CSR_SENVCFG). On VCPU exit (swap_in_host_state, line 763-775), the reverse happens. This correctly virtualizes the S-mode envcfg for the guest and prevents the guest's CBO configuration from leaking into the host.
findings.snippet:
vcpu->arch.host_senvcfg = csr_swap(CSR_SENVCFG, csr->senvcfg);  // guest enter
csr->senvcfg = csr_swap(CSR_SENVCFG, vcpu->arch.host_senvcfg);    // guest exit

findings.finding: No kernel-mode CBO emulation exists for userspace illegal instruction traps. When userspace executes a CBO instruction without proper envcfg bits, the hardware traps it as illegal. The kernel delivers SIGILL to the process. This is the correct behavior: the kernel does not silently emulate CBO instructions that the hardware deems illegal, preserving the envcfg-based security model.

Boot-time envcfg initialization correctly sets CBO enable bits on current->thread.envcfg only when all harts have the extension (riscv_has_extension_unlikely). When some harts lack the extension, a warning is emitted and the bits remain clear. This prevents a situation where a task with CBO envcfg bits set gets scheduled onto a hart without CBO support (which would silently execute CBO instructions as illegal).

CBO block sizes are initialized from DT/ACPI before any CBO instructions can be executed. The validate callbacks (riscv_ext_zicbom_validate, etc.) check that block sizes are present and power-of-2, disabling the extension otherwise. This prevents misconfigured CBO operations with garbage block sizes.
